title: Review 81 Understanding Improvement in Complex Situations Andrew Fell, November 9, 2026
author: SMARTcurriculum Network
source: SMARTcurriculum Weekly Review (SMARTcurriculum Network, Substack), guest reviewer
summary: This week's SMARTcurriculum review, led by guest reviewer Andrew Fell, argues that school improvement should be understood through complexity theory rather than linear cause-and-effect models. It describes schools as ecosystems in which emergence, self-organisation, context sensitivity and layered influence shape outcomes, so that universal recipes give way to cultivating conditions for adaptive change. The instructional core of teacher, student and content is presented as the place where improvement becomes visible, with task design and teacher enactment mattering as much as curriculum intent. A macro, meso and micro model helps leaders see where to intervene, and the piece warns that top-down rollouts, narrow metrics and short snapshots mislead. It closes with leadership habits and a governance checklist: clarify purpose, strengthen task quality, triangulate evidence, run small iterative tests and protect teacher judgment.
points: Treating schools as complex adaptive systems explains why identical initiatives produce different results in different contexts and why change is nonlinear and slow.
Improvement should centre on the quality of pupil tasks and how teachers enact curriculum, since a well-designed curriculum only has impact when adapted skillfully to real students.
Leaders can read improvement across macro (policy), meso (internal conditions) and micro (instructional core) layers to decide where to intervene and how to interpret delayed or mixed results.
Single metrics mislead and invite gaming, so leaders and governors should triangulate data with lesson evidence and pupil voice and track disadvantaged groups longitudinally.
Small, time-bound PDSA-style experiments and protected teacher discretion beat large top-down rollouts.
quotes: Recognising these properties does not mean accepting unpredictability as an excuse. It means shifting from seeking universal recipes to cultivating conditions that enable adaptive, evidence-informed change.
Enactment matters as much as intent: a well-designed curriculum only produces impact when teachers adapt it skillfully to their students.
Indirectness: school-level initiatives require re-contextualisation by teachers before they affect pupils; insufficient support for that process weakens impact.
Narrow metrics: reliance on single indicators can misrepresent systemic improvement and incentivise short-term gaming.
Use triangulated evidence: interpret quantitative metrics alongside classroom observations and pupil voice before making high-stakes decisions.
Ask for triangulated evidence in strategic updates and refuse to make major shifts on single metrics alone.
